Here are my verse-by-verse notes on 2 Kings 13, based on the pages I was able to retrieve and read.

---

## 2 Kings 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1

- **Chronological marker.** Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king over Israel (the northern kingdom) in the 23rd year of Joash king of Judah, reigning 17 years in Samaria. This begins the fulfillment of God's promise to Jehu that his descendants would sit on the throne to the fourth generation (2 Kings 10:30). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **Chronological difficulty:** Josephus and others note the number should likely be the 21st (not 23rd) year, since Jehu reigned 28 years and Joash began in Jehu's 7th year (2 Kings 12:1). The synchronisms of later kings of Israel and Judah are in some confusion. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/13.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/13-1.htm (Pulpit Commentary)
- Gill reconciles by noting that Joash began at the *beginning* of Jehu's 7th year and Jehoahaz began at the beginning of Joash's 23rd. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-13.html
- Clarke suggests Jehoahaz reigned 14 years alone plus 3 years as co-regent with his son Joash. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html

### v. 2

- **The standard condemnation formula:** Jehoahaz "did evil in the sight of the LORD" and followed the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. "The sins of Jeroboam" is almost a technical term in Kings — the counterfeit worship system of golden calves at Bethel and Dan, designed to prevent Israelites from going to Jerusalem. Every northern king was measured by whether he perpetuated this system. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-13-commentary
- Jehoahaz's father Jehu had also continued in this idolatry (2 Kings 10:31); Jehoahaz followed the same path. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/

### v. 3

- **God's anger and Aram's oppression:** Because of Israel's sin, the LORD delivered them into the hands of Hazael king of Aram and his son Ben-hadad. This oppression continued "all their days" — though Gill notes that the Hebrew should read "all *his* days" (Jehoahaz's days), since Israel was later delivered from Ben-hadad (v. 25). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-13.html
- Historically, Assyria normally kept Aram (Syria) weak, but a period of Assyrian internal distraction allowed the Arameans to expand into Israelite territory. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/

### v. 4

- **Jehoahaz's desperate prayer:** The Hebrew literally reads "he stroked the face of the LORD" — a metaphor for seeking favour that also appears in Exodus 32:11 and 1 Kings 13:6. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/13.htm
- Guzik notes the Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be sick," implying weakness and dependency: "Jehoahaz was at the end of his rope." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **God listened — astonishingly.** This is "amazing grace" because Jehoahaz had not truly repented (v. 2). Verses like Isaiah 59:2 say God does not hear those who regard iniquity, yet God listened because of His mercy and because He saw Israel's oppression. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-13-commentary
- Gill: God hearkened not for Jehoahaz's sake or any righteousness of his, but "for the sake of Israel, and because they were oppressed, who were His people." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-13.html
- God's answer was not immediate; Syrian invasions continued throughout Jehoahaz's reign (v. 22), and deliverance came later. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/13.htm

### v. 5

- **"The LORD gave Israel a deliverer"** (literally "a saviour"). Most commentators identify this deliverer as Jehoahaz's son Joash/Jehoash (v. 25), or his grandson Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25–28) — the deliverance came after Jehoahaz had already died. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-13.html
- **Alternative view:** Constable suggests the deliverer was the Assyrian king Adad-Nirari III (810–783 BC), who attacked Damascus and diverted Aram's attention away from Israel. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html
- Guzik: "We don't know the name of this deliverer, but he is well known in heaven. One does not need a great name to do a great work for the LORD." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- Clarke unequivocally identifies the deliverer as Joash, whose successful wars against the Syrians close the chapter. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html

### v. 6

- **No genuine repentance.** "Nevertheless they did not turn away from the sins of the house of Jeroboam." The Asherah pole (wooden image) even remained standing in Samaria, the capital. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- Spurgeon (cited by Guzik): "Israel's repentance was only half-hearted; they repented because they suffered. They repented because of the suffering rather than because of the sin. They went back to the sin after they escaped from the sorrow." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- Clarke identifies the "grove" (KJV) as Asherah/Astarte worship, with "all her abominable rites." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html

### v. 7

- **Military devastation.** Jehoahaz was left with only 50 horsemen, 10 chariots, and 10,000 foot soldiers. The king of Aram had "made them like the dust at threshing" — a vivid image of pulverisation. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- This reduction had begun under Jehu (2 Kings 10:32–36) and continued under Jehoahaz. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html

### vv. 8–9

- Standard closing formula for Jehoahaz's reign. His acts are referred to the "Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel" (a lost royal archive, not the biblical Chronicles). He was buried in Samaria, and his son Joash (Jehoash) succeeded him. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/

### v. 10

- **Jehoash (Joash) son of Jehoahaz** began his reign over Israel in the 37th year of Joash king of Judah, reigning 16 years. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **Chronological issue:** This does not align neatly with v. 1 (if Jehoahaz reigned 17 years from Joash's 23rd year, his death would fall in Joash's 40th year, not the 37th). The LXX reads "39th year." Clarke explains this by a co-regency: Joash son of Jehoahaz was associated with his father in government two years before Jehoahaz's death. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/13.htm
- Constable notes Jehoash ruled the first 5 years as sole ruler and the last 11 as co-regent with his son Jeroboam II. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html

### vv. 11–13

- **The standard evil assessment** — Jehoash "did evil in the sight of the LORD" and walked in the sins of Jeroboam. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **War with Amaziah of Judah:** v. 12 mentions this war; Clarke notes the full account is in 2 Chronicles 25 — Amaziah was totally defeated, taken prisoner, Jerusalem's wall was broken down, and temple and royal treasures were seized. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html
- Jehoash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and his son Jeroboam (Jeroboam II) succeeded him. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/

### v. 14

- **Elisha's final illness.** Even men of faith and miracles are not immune to sickness. God appointed this illness as the means of taking Elisha from the world — unlike Elijah, who was taken up in a whirlwind. Elisha "went the common way of all flesh." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- Clarke estimates Elisha had prophesied about 65 years by this point. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html
- **"My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!"** — These are the same words Elisha himself had cried at Elijah's departure (2 Kings 2:12). Joash recognized that the true strength of Israel was not military hardware but the presence of God's prophet. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- Constable: "The prophet is the man whose prayer is better than chariots and horsemen. Trust in the words of the prophet means that horses and chariots can be abandoned." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html
- Guzik notes the king's weeping seems strange given his evil reign, but Joash "was not a worshipper of false gods; he was a false worshipper of the true God," and had some regard for Elisha. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/

### vv. 15–16

- **The bow and arrows:** A symbolic action. Elisha instructs the king to take a bow and arrows. Elisha then places his hands on the king's hands — symbolising that the king's power in battle would come from Yahweh, whom Elisha represented. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html
- Clarke notes that the bow, arrows, and striking the ground were "all emblematical things, indicative of the deliverance of Israel from Syria." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html

### v. 17

- **"Open the east window"** — eastward toward Syria/Aram, and specifically toward Aphek, the strategic city where Ahab had earlier defeated the Syrians (1 Kings 20:26–30). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **The arrow shot:** Elisha declares it "the LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram." Joash would strike the Arameans at Aphek until they were destroyed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- Clarke notes an ancient custom: shooting an arrow or casting a spear into enemy territory was an emblem of the commencement of hostilities. He cites Alexander the Great throwing a dart into Persian territory, and Virgil's account of Turnus. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html

### vv. 18–19

- **"Strike the ground!"** — Elisha tells Joash to take the remaining arrows and strike the ground. There is scholarly disagreement about whether this means shooting arrows into the ground from the window (Keil, Bähr) or striking the floor with the arrows in hand (Ewald, De Wette, Thenius, supported by the LXX). The contrast between "shoot" (v. 17) and "strike" (v. 18) in Hebrew favours the latter. — https://biblehub.com/2_kings/13-18.htm (Pulpit Commentary)
- **Joash strikes only three times and stops.** This was a test of faith. Elisha was angry because Joash's half-hearted effort — his lack of boldness and persistence — directly limited the scope of Israel's victory. Instead of complete destruction of Aram, Israel would have only three victories. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- Guzik's application: the arrow-shooting models prayer — it requires effort and instruction, is done through an open window (vulnerability before God), aims at a target known only by faith, and loses power when abandoned too soon. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- Constable: "Elisha was angry when Jehoash shot only three more arrows because in doing so the king was demonstrating weak faith. … He failed to trust God even though he knew what God had promised." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html
- **Clarke's alternative view:** "Perhaps it was of the Lord that he smote only thrice, as He had determined to give Israel those three victories only over the Syrians. Elisha's being wroth … does not prove that God was wroth, or that He had intended to give the Syrians five or six overthrows." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html
- **Benson** (Methodist-leaning): If Joash understood the symbolic nature of the action (as the first arrow's meaning had been explained), his stopping at three was "utterly inexcusable" — it showed diffidence in the prophet's promise and greater regard for Syria's strength than God's power. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/2-kings-13.html
- Trapp: "He should have continued smiting till the prophet had said, Enough." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/2-kings-13.html
- **Spurgeon** (cited by Guzik): "It is a fact that God has purposed all things both great and little; neither will anything happen but according to his eternal purpose and decree. It is also a sure and certain fact that, oftentimes, events hang upon the choice of men. Their will has a singular potency." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/

### vv. 20–21

- **Elisha dies and is buried.** Unlike Elijah, he was not taken up in a fiery chariot. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **Moabite raiders** came into the land every spring — marauding bands like those mentioned in 2 Kings 5:2. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html
- **The resurrection miracle:** As Israelites were burying a man, they saw raiders and hastily threw the corpse into Elisha's tomb. When the body touched Elisha's bones, the man revived and stood up. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **Interpretation:** This was a unique, one-time miracle to bring honour to Elisha's memory. There was no inherent power in Elisha's bones; the power was God's. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **Constable:** The miracle demonstrated that God's power worked even through His prophet's corpse, encouraging Jehoash for his battles ahead and rebuking his lack of faith. "Since Elisha was dead there was no question that the power was Yahweh's, not the prophet's." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html
- **Clarke** (Methodist): "This is the first, and I believe the last, account of a true miracle performed by the bones of a dead man; and yet on it and such like the whole system of miraculous working relics has been founded by the popish Church." He is clear that Elisha "did not perform his miracles by any powers of his own, but by the power of God." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html

### vv. 22–23

- **Hazael oppressed Israel throughout Jehoahaz's reign** — this was the discipline God had warned of (2 Kings 8:12 records Elisha's foreknowledge of it). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **God's covenant mercy:** "But the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them … because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- Clarke draws out the Hebrew vocabulary: *vaiyachon* — "tender affection, as a husband has for his wife or a father for his children"; *vairachamem* — "his bowels yearned over them"; *vaiyiphen* — "He turned His face toward them." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html
- **Constable:** "The basis of God's continuing mercy to Israel was not her goodness but God's remaining faithful to the Abrahamic Covenant." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html
- **"As yet"** / "to this day" — Clarke notes that now (in his day, and since the rejection of Christ) they *have* been cast from His presence, but "if they yet turn to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html

### vv. 24–25

- **Hazael dies; Ben-hadad his son succeeds him.** — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **Fulfilment of Elisha's prophecy:** Jehoash son of Jehoahaz recaptured from Ben-hadad the cities Hazael had taken from his father. He defeated Ben-hadad three times — exactly as Elisha had foretold (v. 19). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- Clarke: "Thus God accomplished his word of judgment, and his word of mercy." The recovered cities included Gilead, the territories of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and Bashan (cf. 2 Kings 10:33). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html
- Guzik: "We can suppose that, especially after the third victory, King Joash wished he had shot more arrows through the window at the invitation of Elisha." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/

---

## Points of Difference Between Traditions

### The "Deliverer" of v. 5

- **Traditional evangelical / older commentators** (Gill, Clarke, Guzik, Knapp): The deliverer is Joash (Jehoash) son of Jehoahaz, or Jeroboam II, raised up by God from within Israel.
- **Modern evangelical / dispensational** (Constable): The deliverer may be the Assyrian king Adad-Nirari III, whose attack on Damascus diverted Syrian pressure from Israel — God using a pagan power as His instrument. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html

### The Arrow-Striking: Human Responsibility vs. Divine Sovereignty (vv. 18–19)

- **Spurgeon / Guzik (broadly Reformed Baptist / Charismatic):** Emphasise that "events hang upon the choice of men" — Joash's limited faith directly limited God's blessing. God's promises are sometimes conditional on our faith-filled response. Yet they also hold to God's sovereignty: "God has purposed all things." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
- **Clarke (Methodist/Arminian):** The outcome was divinely determined regardless of Joash's actions. "Perhaps it was of the Lord that he smote only thrice, as He had determined to give Israel those three victories only." Elisha's anger does not necessarily reflect God's anger. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html
- **Benson (Methodist):** Joash's failure was fully his own fault — he was "utterly inexcusable" for diffidence and unbelief. This reflects a more Arminian emphasis on human free response. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/2-kings-13.html

### The Resurrection by Elisha's Bones (v. 21)

- **Protestant** (Clarke, Guzik, Constable): Emphatically deny any inherent power in the bones. It was a unique miracle of God's power to honour Elisha. Clarke explicitly attacks the Catholic doctrine of relics: "on it and such like the whole system of miraculous working relics has been founded by the popish Church." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html
- **Catholic reading:** I was unable to retrieve content from newadvent.org or catholic.com within the search/fetch limits to report the Catholic understanding of this passage and its relationship to the theology of relics.

### The Basis of God's Mercy (v. 23)

- **Reformed / Covenant theology** (Constable, the broader commentary tradition): God's mercy rests entirely on His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — unconditional, sovereign grace. Israel deserved destruction; God was faithful to His own promise. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html
- **Clarke (Methodist):** Also affirms the covenant basis but adds a redemptive-historical note: "the Messiah must come from them, and through them must come that light which is to enlighten the Gentiles, and therefore He would not make an entire end of them." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-13.html

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

- **Constable** (Dallas Theological Seminary): Identifies the "deliverer" of v. 5 with Adad-Nirari III of Assyria rather than an Israelite figure. Also notes H.L. Ellison's suggestion that the resurrected man in v. 21 may only have been *apparently* dead, since burial in that culture happened almost immediately after death. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html
- **Wiseman** (cited by Constable): Compares the arrow-shooting to Joshua's symbolic thrusting of a spear at Ai (Joshua 8:18) — a prophetic symbolic action. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-13.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic Emphasis

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** The arrow-shooting models Spirit-led prayer: it requires boldness, persistence, openness (the "east window"), partnership with God's representative, and faith that acts without knowing the exact outcome. "When God invites us to take something by faith, we must receive it boldly." The application throughout is that half-hearted faith limits what God will do. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-13/
